extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in mathematical exposition and curation of elegant proofs (mathematicians, students, general readers of math books)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria used by the authors of Proofs from THE BOOK for selecting and presenting mathematical proofs—focusing on accessibility, elegance, significance, and presentation for an educated undergraduate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to undergraduate audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected only those that would be accessible to someone with knowledge of basic undergraduate mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors stated they had no definite criteria for what counted as a proof from 'The Book', but chose proofs accessible to readers with basic undergraduate knowledge. Note: some background in algebra, analysis, and topology is required to understand certain parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and brevity of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be brief and elegant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors removed John Leech's proof (that thirteen unit spheres cannot touch a given sphere) from later editions because they could not fill in details in a way that was 'brief and elegant'—illustrating brevity and elegance as selection constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical beauty and aesthetic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection emphasizes 'beauty in mathematics' and proofs worthy of being 'from The Book' (the highest aesthetic praise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the book concerns beauty in mathematics, the authors devoted substantial attention to typography, text appearance, photographs, and illustrations to provide a correspondingly attractive presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance and classical interest of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters are often devoted to particular important theorems, sometimes presenting multiple proofs and related results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many chapters treat classical or noteworthy theorems (e.g., infinity of primes, fundamental theorem of algebra, spectral theorem). Paul Erdős suggested many proofs to include—indicating importance/significance as a selection factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety: multiple proofs and thematic exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Include multiple proofs for the same theorem and, in some cases, explore proofs related to a particular theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book often presents several proofs of a result (e.g., six proofs of the infinity of the primes; four proofs of the Basel problem) and sometimes groups chapters by theme across parts (number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, graph theory). Ziegler accepted that different proofs may be 'perfect' for different readers, reflecting a preference for variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion and subjectivity in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: There were no rigid, formalized criteria; selection relied on the authors' judgment and subjective sense of what constitutes a 'Book' proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly stated they had no definite criteria for what counted as a proof from 'The Book'. Differences between editions (additions, new proofs, occasional deletions) reflect editorial judgement rather than a fixed rubric.
